fixes.explanation: I get why you'd pick him. Isaiah just warned that this king would pour into Judah like a flood (Isaiah 8:7-8). But the LORD says, “Only He should be feared; only He should be dreaded.” (Isaiah 8:13) "He" there is the LORD of Hosts. No king gets in line behind Him.

Isaiah goes the other direction, baker. He says, “I will wait for the LORD… I will put my trust in Him.” (Isaiah 8:17) A couple of verses later he asks, “…shouldn’t a people consult their God instead?” (Isaiah 8:19).

Yes! Isaiah asks, “…shouldn’t a people consult their God instead?” (Isaiah 8:19) It's a question with its answer built in. The mediums and spiritists are the ones who whisper and mutter, and Isaiah points the people to their God instead.

That's the one. Isaiah asks, “Why consult the dead on behalf of the living?” (Isaiah 8:19) That question comes right after he talks about mediums and spiritists. The dead are the ones being consulted, and the living are the ones it's for.

That's what Isaiah says. I think it's a heavy one. “When they are famished, they will become enraged; and looking upward, they will curse their king and their God.” (Isaiah 8:21) It's a hard picture of people at the end of themselves.

The text says the opposite, friend. “Then they will look to the earth and see only distress and darkness and the gloom of anguish. And they will be driven into utter darkness.” (Isaiah 8:22) No dawn shows up in that verse. Just before it, Isaiah says of those who don't speak according to this word, “…they have no light of dawn.” (Isaiah 8:20)

That's the word, baker. Isaiah says, “The people walking in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death, a light has dawned.” (Isaiah 9:2) After the gloom at the end of chapter 8, this is the turn. Light is the whole point.

That's it. Isaiah says, “The people rejoice before You as they rejoice at harvest time, as men rejoice in dividing the plunder.” (Isaiah 9:3) Their joy is compared to the joy of harvest time, and to men dividing the plunder.

That's right. Isaiah says, “For as in the day of Midian You have shattered the yoke of their burden, the bar across their shoulders, and the rod of their oppressor.” (Isaiah 9:4) Three things get shattered: the yoke, the bar and the rod. That's a lot of breaking in one verse.
Nobody's keeping those boots in a closet. Isaiah says they “…will be burned as fuel for the fire.” (Isaiah 9:5) The boots and garments go to the fire, not into storage.

That's right, friend. Isaiah says, “He will reign on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and sustain it with justice and righteousness from that time and forevermore.” (Isaiah 9:7) The throne is David's. The "He" is the one called Wonderful Counselor in the verse before (Isaiah 9:6).
